title: OOM Autopsy–Driven Adaptive Batching and Model De‑escalation
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: We continue to see intermittent OOMs in production clusters under mixed workloads (long-context chat + high-concurrency short requests). Post-mortems show multiple root causes: large KV working sets from long histories, batch admission spikes that exceed per-GPU headroom, and hot-path kernels with unexpectedly large intermediate allocations.

Goal: Build an automated, telemetry-driven mitigation that minimizes customer-visible failures by dynamically adjusting admission/batching/KV policy and gracefully de‑escalating requests to lower-memory model variants when necessary. This ticket implements the control loop and experiment scaffolding (diagnostic collection, decision policy, and model-deescalation ladder).
acceptance_criteria: Reduce production OOM count attributable to KV growth or batch admission by >= 60% in targeted clusters compared to baseline.
End-to-end added latency for P95 generation should not regress more than 15% under typical traffic; P99 acceptable only during active mitigations.
Fallback path (de-escalation to smaller model/quantized variant) must return coherent outputs for 95% of sampled prompts (no catastrophic truncation).
New telemetry fields (oom_cause_tag, admission_fingerprint, kv_eviction_reason) are populated for >= 99% of requests in trial clusters.
Automated canary rollout and rollback documented; rollback must return system to previous behavior within 5 minutes.
implementation_notes: 1) OOM Autopsy collector: lightweight trace attached to OOM events that records admission_fingerprint (batch size, per-request seq_lengths histogram, model variant), kv_snapshot_hash, gpu_mem_snapshot (resident, reserved), and kernel_peak_hint.

2) Admission fingerprinting: per-request fingerprint computed at admission time (short/medium/long bins + priority flag + user-specified soft-limit). Use this to drive dynamic admission caps per GPU worker.

3) Adaptive batching controller: windowed controller that modulates max_batch_size and batch_timeout based on active fingerprints + GPU headroom signal. If headroom < threshold, controller reduces batch_size for fingerprints with largest estimated working set.

4) KV safety-net controller: when headroom is low, trigger prioritized KV trimming: evict cold KV entries from lowest-priority namespaces, optionally snapshot to host if permitted by config. Expose a soft-degradation marker for requests that will lose KV context.

5) Model de‑escalation ladder: maintain model variants in registry (full, quantized-8, distilled-small). Policy: try reduced-batch trimming first, then KV trimming, then route to lower-memory model with metadata marking origin-of-fallback.
6) Circuit-breaker + exponential backoff: if de‑escalation rate exceeds X% or de‑escalation errors increase, open circuit and divert new sessions to dedicated fallback pool while ops investigate.
7) Telemetry and dashboards: Grafana panels for OOM rate by cause, de‑escalation invocations, delta in tokens/sec, and business-level errors. Link alerts to on-call runbook.
8) Feature flags and config: all behaviors behind runtime flags (per-cluster): admission_enabled, kv_trim_threshold, fallback_model_sequence, circuit_thresholds.
9) Testing: unit tests for decision logic, chaos tests injecting fake low-headroom signals, e2e replay using recorded production traces in staging.
10) Backwards compatibility: default behavior is no change; start rollout on non-critical clusters and iterate telemetry thresholds before enabling control loop globally.
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Over-eager KV trimming may degrade output quality for long-session customers. Mitigation: soft flag 'preserve_session' to protect VIP namespaces; gradual rollout and quality regression tracking tied to prompt-sets.

Risk: Frequent model de‑escalation causes user-visible quality drops. Mitigation: prefer batching/KV trim first; require A/B quality checks and an automatic rollback if customer quality metric drops > 5%.
Risk: Decision loop oscillation under bursty traffic. Mitigation: add hysteresis, minimum cooldown window per GPU, and centralized smoothing of headroom signals.
Risk: Telemetry cardinality explosion. Mitigation: sample fingerprints, compress kv_snapshot_hash into buckets, and limit debug traces to sampled OOMs.
test_plan: Unit tests for fingerprint classifier, admission controller, and model-deescalation decision tree.
Staging chaos run: replay 3 representative production traces (chat-heavy, short-request spike, mixed) while toggling kv_trim_threshold and admission caps.
Quality regression harness: run 2k prompt-set against fallback model variants and compare ROUGE/SIM scores; flag regressions > 5%.
Load test: synthetic generators to push GPU headroom below thresholds and assert fallback path triggers and recovers without OOMs.
Canary rollout: start with 1 cluster (non-production), monitor for 48h, expand to 10% traffic, then 50% if stable.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Merge feature flags and instrumentation (no behavior enabled). Deploy to staging.
Phase 1: Enable telemetry + read-only autopsy collector in 1 non-prod cluster; validate fields and dashboards.
Phase 2: Enable adaptive admission and KV safety-net on canary cluster (configured for aggressive sampling). Run for 48h and evaluate metrics.
Phase 3: Enable full control loop with conservative thresholds on 10% production traffic; monitor for 72h. Gradually relax thresholds if safe.
Phase 4: Optional: enable model de‑escalation ladder for sessions where previous mitigations fail; keep strict quality gates and human-in-the-loop for first week.
Rollback: flip global flag to disable control loop. Playbook ensures inflight mitigations drain and system returns to baseline within 5 minutes.
